_: Provenance for the generated footage in clipsrc/generated/.
Every clip is image-to-video conditioned on TWO approved plates: `from` is
its first frame and `to` is its last. That is not a stylistic choice, it is
what makes the footage safe to drop into this table. VIDEO.md section 6 asks
for the first frame to be locked to an approved plate so drift is bounded
inside one clip; locking the last frame as well means a clip also ENDS on a
picture that already exists as a still, so <Clip> can cut away to it with no
jump and a browser that cannot play the video shows the right frame anyway.
These models are not deterministic and the seed is not exposed, so this file
records how a clip was ordered, not how to reproduce it byte for byte. The
mp4 in clipsrc/generated/ is the source asset; this is its receipt.
Re-fetch with: node scripts/fetch-generated.mjs [name...]
reshot: TEN OF THE TWELVE CLIPS BELOW WERE RE-SHOT, and the reason is the only
piece of feedback in this project that no measurement could have produced.
A player came back from the preview and said the saloon looked like an
audience: machine_lean was fifteen men in a wall staring straight down the
lens and machine_roar was the whole room with its hats in the air, and
those are the two pictures a player looks at most. He was right, and it is
worth being precise about what was wrong, because the first instinct - make
the crowd smaller - is not it.
The defect was that everybody in the room was pointed at the same thing.
A saloon is not a theatre. Most of the people in one have not noticed the
machine, are mid-sentence with somebody else, are dealing a hand, or are
waiting for a drink; the two or three nearest it react and the rest of the
evening does not pause. So every prompt below now says that twice - once as
what the reacting people do, and once as a list of what the room does NOT
do: nobody stands up, nobody throws a hat, no rows of fists go up, no wall
of faces appears, and the room does not turn around.
That also makes the picture agree with the mix for the first time. The
reactions in src/audio/crowd.ts were pulled back to two or three throats a
round earlier, in answer to a different complaint, and the footage was
still showing a stadium over the top of them.
The two that were not re-shot are intro_bar and intro_band, whose plates
did not change: intro_bar was already a room where everybody is doing
something, and intro_band is a macro of a paper reel strip with no people
in it at all.
Previous take ids are kept on each clip so the old footage stays orderable.
conditioned-on-aligned: THE NINE MACHINE CLIPS ARE CONDITIONED ON clipsrc/aligned/, NOT ON THE RAW
PLATES BESIDE THIS FILE, and the first attempt at the re-shoot got that
wrong in a way worth writing down, because nothing about it is visible and
both measurements that caught it blamed something else.
The first nine re-orders used clipsrc/machine_*.jpg as their start and end
references - the obvious choice, since those are the approved plates. The
footage came back looking right and failed two checks. verify:lock said the
rim was moving 3.85-5.29 against a limit of 3.5, and verify:identity said
every clip's FIRST frame was 14-15 off its plate while every LAST frame was
fine at 1.15-3.08. A first frame that is wrong and a last frame that is
right is a strange shape for drift, and it is not drift.
Measuring the ends directly gave the answer:
pull frame 0 vs RAW clipsrc/machine_rest.jpg           3.39 / 2.21
pull frame 0 vs ALIGNED clipsrc/aligned/machine_rest.png   17.34 / 15.09
raw jpg vs aligned png                                 18.22 / 15.27
The take was a faithful reproduction of the plate it was given. It was
given the wrong plate. align-plates.mjs shifts each plate, then crops
MARGIN=18 off every side and rescales back to 1280x720 - about a 2.9% zoom
that the whole set shares so the geometry in src/machine.ts describes all of
them. build-clips.mjs registers frames against the ALIGNED plate, and its
registration is translation-only by design, so a 2.9% scale difference is
the one error it structurally cannot take out. lock.mjs then pushed every
frame around trying to, which is why the rim jittered.
So the five machine plates were run through align-plates.mjs, the results
converted to JPEG, uploaded, and the nine clips ordered again against those.
verify-identity.mjs already says as much in its own comments - the aligned
plate 'is what the conditioning used anyway' - and now that is true.
The three opening plates are exempt and were not re-ordered on this account:
align-plates.mjs copies them through with scale only and no crop, because
they are their own cameras with nothing registered to them, so raw and
aligned are the same picture.
chosen: Kling 3 Omni over PixVerse V6, decided by measurement rather than taste.
Both were given the identical rest->pull pair and the identical prompt, and
scripts/measure-drift.mjs was run over every frame of each result:
worst translation   mean residual   source   credits
Translation is the column that mattered. The reel window is a hole the DOM
bands show through, so a casting that wanders is bands leaking past the
brass, and while scripts/lib/lock.mjs takes the wander out afterwards, the
less there is to take out the less the frame has to be pushed around. The
residuals are effectively tied, and both sit at about the level the approved
still plates already differ from each other by, which is the real bar.

_: The four shots below are the opening, and they are the one place in this
project where the camera is allowed to move. Everything at the table is

opening has nothing laid over it, so it can be a camera instead of a

They exist to replace pushIn(), a Ken Burns crop that stood in for a
dolly. A crop of a still cannot produce parallax, so the fake move read
as a zoom on a photograph, and it was also the thing blowing the first
screen budget: the synthetic motion had no real structure to predict
from, so intro.sm.webm encoded at 726 KB against a 400 KB ceiling.

intro_bar.prompt:
A slow, steady dolly drifting forward and slightly to the right along the length of the bar in a crowded 1899 saloon at night. The camera moves at an unhurried walking pace, as if it has just come through the door into the noise of the room. No handheld shake, no cuts.

The room is alive and everyone in it is doing something. The men along the brass rail talk to each other with real movement - heads turning, mouths working, hands gesturing, shoulders shifting as they lean in to be heard. Two of them raise glasses and touch them together. The bartender in the white apron tips the bottle and pours into the row of shot glasses on the bar top. The man at the piano works his hands along the keys. The man beside him laughs, head back. Somebody drains a beer and sets it down on the wood. Cigar smoke rolls slowly through the beams of the hanging oil lamps, and the lamp flames gutter and steady.

Keep the exposure and grade exactly as the first frame: warm amber pools falling off hard into near-black, thick smoke, heavy 35mm film grain, shallow depth of field. Nobody walks into or out of frame and nobody looks at the camera. No text or lettering appears. No cuts.

_: Re-shot twice now, and the two rewrites are worth reading together
because the second one reverses the first one's conclusion.
The original travelled down an EMPTY hall - 'past abandoned card tables
and an empty faro layout' - which was the deliberate opposite of what
the table wanted: the room is the thing the player is playing against,
and it spent the opening dead. So the plate became a full room and the
shot was rebuilt around a contrast: a noisy hall with one SILENT knot of
people packed around the machine at the dead end, watching it.
That knot is exactly what a player then objected to, and he was right.
It is the establishing shot of the whole game, so whatever it says about
this room is what the room means for the next twenty minutes, and what
it said was 'people come here to watch this machine'. They do not. It
is a bar with a machine in the corner of it.
So the plate was made again (the card game is now in the foreground
where the empty tables used to be) and the shot inverts its own point:
ONE man stands at the machine, alone, working it himself, and nobody in
the room looks at him. The machine is still the brightest thing in frame
and the eye is still drawn down the floor to it - but because of the
light, not because anyone is looking.
